analysis.one_liner: Requires online marketplaces to verify and disclose the identity of their high-volume third-party sellers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee from its introduction in July 2020 until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required online marketplaces to collect and verify bank account, government ID, tax ID, and contact information from third-party sellers who make 200 or more transactions totaling $5,000 or more in a year, and to show the seller's name, address, and contact information on product listings. It also would have required a conspicuous way for shoppers to report suspicious activity, with the Federal Trade Commission enforcing the rules. It died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Online shoppers, especially people buying goods from third-party sellers on large marketplaces. Today a listing may not tell you who is actually selling you the product; the bill would have forced marketplaces to verify who high-volume sellers really are and display their name, address, and contact information, and to give shoppers an easy way to flag suspicious activity. Legitimate sellers would also benefit from a marketplace where anonymous bad actors cannot hide.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Online shoppers buying from third-party sellers

how_it_helps.text: Marketplaces would have to collect and verify a high-volume seller's bank account information, government-issued photo ID, tax identification number, and contact information within days of the seller crossing the threshold, and re-verify any changes.

Sellers' full name, physical address, whether they also manufacture or resell goods, and working contact information would have to be displayed conspicuously on their product listings, so shoppers know who they are buying from.
Every high-volume seller's listing would have to include a conspicuous electronic and telephone mechanism for reporting suspicious marketplace activity.
If a marketplace warehouses or ships a product, it would have to disclose the identity of the actual high-volume seller supplying it when that differs from the listed seller.
The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the requirements as an unfair or deceptive practice, with the same powers and penalties it has under the FTC Act.

analysis.who_pays: Online marketplaces (platforms like Amazon, eBay, and Facebook Marketplace) would bear the cost of building and running identity and bank-account verification systems, and high-volume third-party sellers would bear the cost of submitting documentation and keeping it current. Some of those compliance costs would likely be passed on to shoppers through fees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Online marketplaces and their third-party sellers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on platforms and small sellers: the threshold of 200 transactions or $5,000 in revenue over 12 months pulls in relatively small sellers, who would have to submit government photo ID and bank account information and re-certify annually or be suspended.

The bill is built around collecting and displaying personal data, which raises privacy concerns. It softens this with carve-outs — a home-based seller can withhold a residential street address and a seller with only a personal phone number can withhold it — but that means shoppers get less information in exactly the cases where sellers are individuals.
Enforcement relies entirely on the Federal Trade Commission; a shopper who was deceived by an undisclosed seller could not sue under this bill, so protection depends on the FTC choosing to act.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are real but modest and targeted: verification paperwork for small sellers, system-building costs for platforms, and privacy trade-offs that the bill partially addresses with carve-outs for home addresses and personal phone numbers. The benefit — shoppers knowing who is actually selling them goods, and a phone-and-web route to report suspicious listings — is a straightforward transparency gain. This is a reasonably designed consumer-disclosure bill, not a heavy-handed one; the main honest objection is the paperwork burden on small sellers near the threshold.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on July 23, 2020, joined by Rep. Kathy Castor, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The bill never advanced past that referral — no committee vote, no report, no floor action — and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online marketplaces avoided new verification and disclosure mandates, and high-volume sellers kept selling without having to reveal their identity to shoppers. Consumers got none of the promised transparency.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Online marketplaces and anonymous high-volume sellers

against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — after it was referred on the day of introduction.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only sign of support was bipartisan but tiny — the Democratic sponsor, one additional Democratic cosponsor, and one Republican cosponsor.

industries.industry: Online marketplaces (Amazon, eBay, Facebook Marketplace, Etsy and similar platforms)
industries.note: The bill would have forced platforms to build systems to verify the bank accounts, government IDs, and tax IDs of their high-volume third-party sellers and to display seller identities on product listings. That means compliance spending and a hit to revenue from anonymous or hard-to-trace sellers — the opposite of what platforms want, even though shopper trust might improve.

Legitimate sellers would face new paperwork — government ID, bank details, annual certification — and public display of their name and address. Sellers who profit from anonymity, such as those moving counterfeit or misdescribed goods, would lose their ability to hide; all sellers would gain something from a marketplace where shoppers can see who they are dealing with.

The bill explicitly lets marketplaces satisfy the verification rules by contracting with payment processors or third-party identity-verification services, creating new demand for those companies' services in service of consumer transparency.
